blueprints.title: Engineered tissues & repair
blueprints.query: engineered cartilage skin vascular graft functional clinical trial
blueprints.question: When does an engineered tissue restore durable function in an aging or damaged body?
blueprints.who: Keep human graft trials, perfused constructs and animal implants distinct.
blueprints.what: Engineered cartilage, skin, blood vessels and muscle with measurable structure and function.
blueprints.where: Vascular supply, extracellular matrix, host interface and immune compatibility.
blueprints.when: Early graft survival, healing speed and function months or years later are separate outcomes.
blueprints.why: Cell survival and a tissue-like shape do not guarantee mechanical or physiological function.
blueprints.how: Compare graft maturation, perfusion, donor-site demand, integration and patient-relevant function from primary trials and experimental tissue datasets.
blueprints.falsifier: A graft survives but heals slowly, loses function, scars or fails mechanical integration.
blueprints.desired_changes: Improve functional integration and durable repair, including tests of genome-corrected engineered tissue.

blueprints.title: Nanomedicine & tissue delivery
blueprints.query: targeted lipid nanoparticle base editing extrahepatic senolytic aged mice
blueprints.question: Can a carrier deliver enough active cargo to the intended aging tissue while limiting other-tissue exposure?
blueprints.who: Separate cultured human cells, aged animals and treated patients.
blueprints.what: Lipid nanoparticles, extracellular vesicles, liposomes and other targeted carriers for editors or damage-modifying cargo.
blueprints.where: Distinguish whole-organ accumulation, uptake by the intended cell type and intracellular cargo release.
blueprints.when: Measure hours-long distribution, weeks-long function and durable effects separately.
blueprints.why: A fluorescent carrier signal does not prove editing, selective senolysis or lasting rejuvenation.
blueprints.how: Compare biodistribution, target-cell editing or cargo activity, functional endpoints, dose-response and adverse observations in primary studies.
blueprints.falsifier: Target-organ fluorescence without target-cell action, or benefit offset by toxicity or poor coverage.
blueprints.desired_changes: Improve tissue and cell targeting with reproducible functional readouts and explicit delivery gaps.

blueprints.title: Glycation & tissue resilience
blueprints.question: Can carbonyl stress be reduced while preserving useful signaling and tissue function?
blueprints.who: Compare healthy adults, metabolic disease cohorts, cells and animal models separately.
blueprints.what: Carnosine and related histidine-containing dipeptides; carbonyl scavenging and glycation hypotheses.
blueprints.where: Circulating markers versus long-lived extracellular matrix; tissue exposure is a separate question.
blueprints.when: Distinguish prevention of new damage from reversal of established damage.
blueprints.why: Lower circulating glycation markers might not remove existing tissue crosslinks.
blueprints.how: Retrieve human and mechanistic studies; resolve carnosine, anserine and homocarnosine; compare structures and conformer sensitivity.
blueprints.falsifier: Biomarker changes without measurable improvement in the tissue endpoint, or no exposure at the target tissue.
blueprints.desired_changes: Explore stability and polarity hypotheses while keeping carbonyl-reactive chemistry under scrutiny.

blueprints.title: Muscle & metabolic tradeoffs
blueprints.question: Which metabolic improvements are compatible with preserving muscle mass and training adaptation?
blueprints.who: Keep older-adult training trials distinct from healthy young adults and people with diabetes.
blueprints.what: Metformin, mTOR/AMPK signaling, incretin therapies and muscle outcomes.
blueprints.where: Skeletal muscle, liver and systemic metabolic regulation.
blueprints.when: Acute signaling versus adaptation over months; longevity remains a separate endpoint.
blueprints.why: An intervention can improve one endpoint while impairing another.
blueprints.how: Compare randomized body-composition and training studies, lean mass, strength and physical function; retain null and adverse outcomes.
blueprints.falsifier: Improved metabolic markers paired with loss of strength, lean tissue or training responsiveness.
blueprints.desired_changes: Separate desired metabolic effects from muscle-growth suppression; no single anti-aging score.

blueprints.title: Metabolic aging & brain health
blueprints.query: metabolic aging cognitive decline GLP-1 randomized
blueprints.question: Do metabolic interventions preserve cognitive function with age, and is the proposed mechanism tested?
blueprints.who: People with diabetes or obesity, neurodegenerative disease models, and healthy adults are separate populations.
blueprints.what: Metabolic, vascular and inflammatory interventions with objective cognitive and disease endpoints.
blueprints.where: Brain exposure, peripheral metabolism and inflammatory signaling.
blueprints.when: Transient subjective effects versus durable cognitive performance or disease incidence.
blueprints.why: Reduced glucose variability is a mechanism hypothesis, not proof of cognitive enhancement.
blueprints.how: Retrieve trials and observational studies; separate test performance from dementia diagnosis; collect anecdotes with cointerventions and identity uncertainty.
blueprints.falsifier: Association disappears after confounder control, or no functional benefit despite biomarker change.
blueprints.desired_changes: Investigate exposure and selectivity hypotheses; descriptors alone cannot predict brain penetration.

blueprints.title: Senescence & immune clearance
blueprints.question: Can harmful senescent cells be cleared while preserving beneficial senescence and tissue repair?
blueprints.who: Aged and disease-model animals first; human evidence must be identified independently.
blueprints.what: uPAR-directed CAR-T, senolytic small molecules and senomorphic approaches.
blueprints.where: Target antigen distribution across tissues and cell states.
blueprints.when: Durability, recurrence of senescence and long-term immune consequences.
blueprints.why: A shared marker may be present on cells that should be preserved.
blueprints.how: Map primary studies, target-expression datasets and functional endpoints; inspect selectivity and adverse observations.
blueprints.falsifier: Off-target cell loss, impaired repair, or senescence-marker reduction without functional benefit.
blueprints.desired_changes: Improve tissue and cell-state specificity as a research objective; no engineered-cell construction protocol.

blueprints.title: Somatic mutations & genome repair
blueprints.query: somatic mutation aging tissues base editing functional repair
blueprints.question: Which age-acquired DNA changes impair tissue function, and what fraction of affected cells would need correction to recover it?
blueprints.who: Compare normal human tissues, disease models and edited patients by age and cell type.
blueprints.what: Somatic single-base variants, indels, clone behavior, base-editing evidence and epigenetic state as a parallel variable.
blueprints.where: Map mutation classes and clonal burden by tissue and cell type; mitochondrial DNA is a separate target.
blueprints.when: Distinguish prevention of new mutations, correction of existing ones and long-term clonal selection.
blueprints.why: Epigenetic reprogramming changes cell state but does not itself rewrite a mutated DNA base.
blueprints.how: Connect single-cell mutation maps to measured cell phenotypes; compare target coverage, delivery fraction, editing fraction and functional rescue across primary studies.
blueprints.falsifier: Sequence correction without functional rescue, or selection and off-target changes that worsen tissue outcomes.
blueprints.desired_changes: Prioritize causal lesions and tissue function while tracking genome and epigenome independently.

blueprints.title: Replacement organs & integration
blueprints.query: bioprinted kidney liver vascularization functional transplantation
blueprints.question: What prevents printed or grown tissue from replacing a full-size functional organ?
blueprints.who: Organoids, engineered constructs, animal transplantation and human recipients are distinct stages.
blueprints.what: Bioprinting, vascularization, maturation, immune compatibility and transplant integration.
blueprints.where: Perfusion, collecting systems, nerves and interfaces with host tissue.
blueprints.when: Viability in culture versus months of stable integrated organ function.
blueprints.why: Correct geometry and cell survival do not establish complete organ function.
blueprints.how: Link primary datasets to the existing oxygen/perfusion tools; model transport with explicit measured or illustrative parameters.
blueprints.falsifier: Necrotic regions, incomplete maturation, thrombosis or failure of the organ-specific functional endpoint.
blueprints.desired_changes: Improve transport, architecture and integration independently; robotic transplantation remains a separate engineering program.

blueprints.title: Skin, hair & structural restoration
blueprints.query: scar regeneration skin appendages wound healing
blueprints.question: Can tissue be restored with normal architecture and appendages rather than only a changed visual appearance?
blueprints.who: Human clinical studies, animal wound models and engineered tissues remain separate.
blueprints.what: Scar remodeling, skin regeneration, hair follicles, dental structures and aesthetic restoration.
blueprints.where: Epidermis, dermis, extracellular matrix, appendages and supporting structures.
blueprints.when: Early closure versus mature scarring and long-term durability.
blueprints.why: Scarless appearance and complete biological restoration are different endpoints.
blueprints.how: Retrieve source-specific images, histology and functional measures; track applicability across injury types and ages.
blueprints.falsifier: Improved appearance with impaired barrier function, abnormal architecture or recurrence.
blueprints.desired_changes: Compare cosmetic, structural and functional outcomes independently.

blueprints.title: Experimental compound leads
blueprints.query: experimental geroprotector epitalon thymalin clinical trial
blueprints.question: Which informal claims can be turned into specific, falsifiable research hypotheses?
blueprints.who: Record species, population and whether a report is self-described.
blueprints.what: Epitalon, thymalin, SARMs and other user-selected experimental leads.
blueprints.where: Specify the proposed tissue and measurable endpoint for each claim.
blueprints.when: Immediate subjective effects versus persistent objective effects.
blueprints.why: Forum and vendor reports can reveal questions while containing selection, commercial and identity biases.
blueprints.how: Search literature, registries and public web leads; preserve source type, missing information, cointerventions and contradictory reports.
blueprints.falsifier: No objective signal, unverified compound identity, duplicated anecdotes or results limited to a different population.
blueprints.desired_changes: Explore structural neighbors and submitted modifications; retain rejected candidates and unknowns.

findings.title: Carnosine: a positive biomarker result
findings.claim: A randomized study in 54 adults with type 2 diabetes reported improvements in circulating carboxymethyl lysine and HbA1c over 12 weeks.
findings.boundary: No demonstrated reversal of established tissue crosslinks or human aging.

findings.title: Carnosine: a null result in a different population
findings.claim: A randomized study in 36 autistic children found no significant change in measured plasma AGE or lipoxidation-precursor concentrations.
findings.boundary: Different population and study conditions; this is not a direct replication of the diabetes study.

findings.title: Metformin can conflict with a muscle endpoint
findings.claim: The MASTERS trial in 94 adults aged 65 and older found smaller lean and thigh muscle mass gains during resistance training with metformin; strength differences were not significant.
findings.boundary: This does not establish the effect in younger healthy adults.

findings.title: Tirzepatide: fat loss also included lean tissue
findings.claim: In the 160-participant SURMOUNT-1 DXA substudy, fat mass fell 33.9% and lean mass 10.9%; about one quarter of lost weight was lean mass.
findings.boundary: DXA lean tissue includes water and nonmuscle tissues. This is not evidence of muscle anabolism.

findings.title: A cognition lead, with causal uncertainty
findings.claim: A retrospective diabetes-cohort analysis reported a lower dementia hazard with tirzepatide than semaglutide: HR 0.69, 95% CI 0.48-0.99.
findings.boundary: Observational diagnosis data do not establish cognitive enhancement or mediation by glucose variability.

findings.title: Senolytic CAR-T has functional mouse evidence
findings.claim: uPAR-targeting CAR-T cells improved exercise capacity and glucose tolerance in aged or metabolically stressed mouse models.
findings.boundary: The study does not demonstrate human rejuvenation or universal target selectivity.

findings.title: OSK: tissue-specific functional recovery
findings.claim: Mouse retinal studies reported axon regeneration and recovery of visual function with OSK expression in injury, glaucoma and aging models.
findings.boundary: Not whole-body reversal and not evidence that accumulated DNA-sequence mutations were repaired.

findings.title: Transient reprogramming can also produce tumors
findings.claim: A separate in-vivo mouse reprogramming study produced tumors containing undifferentiated dysplastic cells.
findings.boundary: Different constructs and experimental conditions from targeted recovery studies; model identity matters.

findings.title: Epithalamin: a striking but narrow historical clinical signal
findings.claim: A randomized comparative follow-up of 39 older coronary patients given epithalamin and 40 controls reported lower cardiovascular aging measures and 28% fewer deaths after 12 years.
findings.boundary: Small, older, disease-specific study from one research program; the abstract does not give enough design detail to evaluate allocation, attrition or independent replication. Epithalamin extract evidence cannot automatically be assigned to synthetic Epitalon or vendor products.

findings.title: Epitalon extends telomeres in cell models, including cancer lines
findings.claim: A 2025 study reported telomere extension and telomerase changes in normal epithelial and fibroblast lines, and telomere extension associated with ALT activity in two breast cancer cell lines.
findings.boundary: Cell-culture finding only; no whole-body aging outcome. The journal later corrected Figures 1-3 (PMID 41240216), so the corrected article and methods should be checked before interpreting magnitudes.

findings.title: Thymalin and Epithalamin: historical mortality claims need design review
findings.claim: A 2003 report describes clinical observations of thymic and pineal peptide bioregulators in 266 older people and reports lower mortality across treatment groups over 6-8 years.
findings.boundary: The abstract does not describe randomization or enough methods to assess confounding and attrition; products were peptide bioregulators, not evidence for every modern synthetic or vendor-labeled peptide.

findings.title: Enobosarm increased lean mass in a short phase II trial
findings.claim: A 12-week double-blind phase II trial in 120 healthy men over 60 and postmenopausal women reported dose-dependent lean-mass gains and an improvement in physical function for GTx-024 (enobosarm).
findings.boundary: One investigational molecule and a short trial in older adults; it does not establish effects in young bodybuilders or the long-term safety of enobosarm or other SARMs. The sponsor employed a study author.

findings.title: FDA warning covers products marketed as SARMs
findings.claim: FDA states SARMs are not approved and describes reports of serious or life-threatening events, including liver injury and cardiovascular risks.
findings.boundary: Regulatory safety information is not a molecule-specific trial; online product identity and purity add uncertainty.

findings.title: Retatrutide has phase III diabetes results
findings.claim: In a 40-week randomized phase III trial of 537 adults with type 2 diabetes, retatrutide reduced HbA1c and mean bodyweight fell 11.5-15.3% across treatment groups, versus 2.6% with placebo.
findings.boundary: The population had type 2 diabetes and inadequate control with diet and exercise alone. The trial did not establish muscle anabolism, cognitive enhancement or slower aging.

findings.title: Base editing corrected the causal progeria mutation in mice
findings.claim: An adenine base editor corrected the LMNA mutation in patient-derived cells and HGPS mice; treatment at postnatal day 14 extended median lifespan in one mouse cohort from 215 to 510 days.
findings.boundary: This corrects one known, high-effect mutation in a rare accelerated-aging disease model. It does not demonstrate repair of the diverse somatic mutations accumulated in ordinary aging or human rejuvenation.

findings.title: Progeria bone editing showed a narrow timing window
findings.claim: A September 2026 HGPS mouse study reported partial bone rescue; mutation correction was about 22% after treatment at postnatal day 14, about 10% at one month and below 1% at four months.
findings.boundary: A monogenic progeria model and AAV9-delivered editor; the timing dependence highlights delivery and disease-stage limits for translation to ordinary aging.

findings.title: NSI-189 phase II: a mixed cognitive signal
findings.claim: In a 220-participant randomized phase II trial in major depressive disorder, NSI-189 did not significantly improve the primary depression endpoint versus placebo. Some CogScreen secondary measures favored one treatment arm, while Cogstate measures did not show a corresponding signal.
findings.boundary: This was a depression-treatment study, not a trial of healthy-person cognitive enhancement; secondary test findings need prespecified replication.

findings.title: A kidney scaffold maintained blood perfusion for seven days
findings.claim: In a small porcine study, re-endothelialized decellularized kidney grafts averaged 87.7%, 80.9% and 68.5% perfusion on days 0, 3 and 7, respectively; native-kidney controls averaged 98.4%. The differences were not statistically significant.
findings.boundary: This measured vascular patency, not filtration or replacement-kidney function. It does not establish durable graft integration or stable endothelial coverage.

findings.title: Human kidney cells enabled short-term filtration in a pig graft
findings.claim: Human endothelial cells and podocytes repopulated a decellularized porcine kidney scaffold. In heterotopic pig implants, grafts produced urine with filtration indices; the longest reported observation was five hours in one graft.
findings.boundary: Acute proof of concept with very small numbers. The constructs lacked tubular epithelial cells, so tubular reabsorption and full kidney function were not tested; the grafts did not replace the animals' native kidneys.

findings.title: Follicle transplantation remodeled some mature human scars
findings.claim: A small human pilot found epidermal and dermal remodeling after anagen hair-follicle transplantation in three people with mature scalp scars; a separate split-thickness skin-graft scar was also examined.
findings.boundary: Very small, localized, non-randomized pilot evidence. It does not establish scarless healing, complete scar removal, or restoration of youthful appearance or function across other scar types.

findings.title: uPAR CAR-T also has a distinct preclinical oncology signal
findings.claim: A 2026 study reported that uPAR-directed CAR-T cells attacked malignant and supportive stromal populations across preclinical solid-tumor models, with activity in humanized-mouse systems.
findings.boundary: This is preclinical oncology evidence, not a human treatment result and not evidence that broad uPAR targeting is safe for senescent-cell clearance in aging tissues.

findings.title: Caloric restriction reduced mutation burden in some mouse tissues
findings.claim: Duplex sequencing of 36 mice at 19 months found about 29% fewer somatic substitutions in bulk liver, 15% fewer in kidney and 39% fewer in hepatocytes under caloric restriction; the neuron contrast was not significant.
findings.boundary: This measured mutation prevention or accumulation, not correction of existing variants. The two restricted-feeding schedules differed in reported lifespan but not detectably in substitution burden; mutation reduction alone does not explain longevity.

findings.title: Age-related clones have different cellular phenotypes
findings.claim: Joint single-cell DNA and RNA profiling of phenotypically normal aged esophagus from six people linked NOTCH1-mutant clones to stunted epithelial differentiation and TP53-mutant clones to increased cycling and altered differentiation.
findings.boundary: Small, tissue-specific observational map. A mutation or expanding clone is not automatically a damage target; causal tissue-level benefit from editing these clones was not tested.

findings.title: Clinical base correction: one monogenic case, short follow-up
findings.claim: A patient-specific lipid-nanoparticle base editor was given to an infant with CPS1 deficiency. Over seven weeks after initial treatment, more dietary protein was tolerated and nitrogen-scavenger medication was halved.
findings.boundary: One infant with a known inherited mutation, not age-acquired genome damage. No human tissue-editing fraction or long-term rejuvenation outcome was reported.

findings.title: Full reprogramming does not erase somatic sequence variants
findings.claim: Sequencing of human induced-pluripotent-stem-cell clones found substantial somatic variation, including pre-existing mutations and selection of cancer-associated variants during culture.
findings.boundary: Cultured full reprogramming is not the same as partial in-vivo epigenetic reprogramming. It illustrates why genome sequence and epigenetic state need separate measurements.

findings.title: Mature engineered cartilage improved a two-year knee outcome
findings.claim: In a randomized phase II trial of focal knee defects, mature nasal-chondrocyte engineered cartilage produced a median KOOS of 85 versus 79 for a less-mature cell-activated matrix at 24 months; the adjusted difference was 7.27 points.
findings.boundary: An open-label active-comparator trial for focal defects, not reversal of diffuse osteoarthritis or whole-body aging. The patient-reported score does not alone establish lifelong graft durability.

findings.title: Engineered skin improved scar quality but closed more slowly
findings.claim: In a 23-person intra-patient randomized phase II trial, bio-engineered autologous skin had a better observer scar score at three months (23.4 versus 27.9) and greater coverage per donor area (8.5 versus 0.9) than split-thickness grafts.
findings.boundary: Median wound closure took 60.5 versus 22 days, and early graft take was 69.8% versus 85.0%. This is reconstruction of defects, not scar-free or age-reversed skin.
findings.design: Human randomized intra-patient phase II trial

findings.title: Corrected progeria cells restored functions in engineered vessels
findings.claim: Base-edited patient-derived vascular cells yielded perfused tissue-engineered vessels with restored vasodilation and smooth-muscle density; constructs starting with at least 50% edited smooth-muscle cells improved several markers.
findings.boundary: An in-vitro human tissue model of one monogenic accelerated-aging disorder. It does not show transplantation, correction of normal age-acquired mutations or clinical vascular rejuvenation.

findings.title: Lung-targeted nanoparticles delivered base correction to stem cells
findings.claim: Intravenous lipid nanoparticles corrected a CFTR mutation in about 50% of isolated lung basal stem cells in a mouse model and restored chloride function in patient-derived airway cells in vitro.
findings.boundary: The whole-lung editing fraction was much lower than the isolated stem-cell fraction. The long 660-day persistence result used a separate reporter model, not demonstrated long-term rescue of mutant CFTR or aging damage.

findings.title: A nanosenolytic improved short-term function in aged mice
findings.claim: An experimental nanoparticle senolytic lowered senescence-associated signals in liver, lung and kidney and improved treadmill and grip measures in 18-month-old mice over an eight-week experiment.
findings.boundary: Physical-function groups were small (n=5). Carrier biodistribution signal is not proof of selective intracellular action, and no human or lifespan benefit was shown.

findings.title: Targeted vesicles carried senolytics to aged adipose tissue
findings.claim: Peptide-functionalized extracellular vesicles carrying dasatinib and quercetin reduced adipose inflammatory signals and produced modest physical-performance improvements in naturally aged mice.
findings.boundary: Small, short animal study; vesicle localization does not itself establish cargo release or target-cell selectivity. No maximal-speed improvement, human outcome or longevity result was shown.

findings.title: Bioengineered retinal implant reached older patients
findings.claim: A phase I/IIa study implanted a stem-cell-derived retinal-pigment-epithelium monolayer on a scaffold in 15 older adults with advanced geographic atrophy; four treated eyes gained more than five visual-acuity letters at one year.
findings.boundary: Single-arm safety study with a non-significant fellow-eye comparison, not demonstrated efficacy. Serious ocular events occurred in early recipients; tissue implantation did not restore normal vision.

findings.title: Brain-endothelial nanosenolytic changed barrier markers in aged rats
findings.claim: In naturally aged rats, a navitoclax-loaded senescence-responsive nanoparticle reduced brain-endothelial senescence markers and blood-brain-barrier leakage and improved an exploratory-behavior measure versus vehicle.
findings.boundary: Small animal groups, a behavioral surrogate rather than proven cognitive recovery, and unresolved local-versus-systemic mechanism. Lower administered payload across different routes does not establish a 250-fold safety gain; no lifespan or human outcome was measured.
